newsitem.title: USA: Illinois crash investigators probe radio traffic.
newsitem.headline: Illinois crash investigators probe radio traffic.

text.p: The last radio message heard from the pilot of a small plane prior to a fiery collision with another plane that killed 14 people was that he was holding at a runway in preparation for takeoff, investigators said Friday.

Any subsequent message issued by the pilot of the twin-prop Beech King Air 200 was not audible to another pilot listening in on the common radio frequency, National Transportation Board investigators said.

NTSB spokesman Pat Cariseo said investigators interviewed the pilot of the third aircraft, who was listening in on radio traffic as he waited to take off behind the King Air plane. He told them the United Express pilot had radioed from 10 miles out that he was on approach and ready to land.

He did not hear the King Air pilot radio a message of his intention to take off but such a broadcast might have been "stepped on" -- obscured by a simultaneous radio transmission from elsewhere, safety board investigators said.

The smaller plane broadsided the United Express turboprop Beech 1900 at the intersection of two runways, killing 12 people on board the commuter plane and two people in the King Air craft in an explosion and fire.
Quincy's Baldwin Field is one of hundreds of small U.S. airports without control towers where pilots use a common radio frequency and visual checks to clear landings and takeoffs among themselves.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association said in Washington Thursday that the Quincy crash spotlighted the potential risks of flying into increasingly busy unmanned airports. It called for federal regulators to investigate.
Cariseo said the issue of airports that lack control towers was one of several investigators were examining in light of the Quincy crash.
